values.value: MCP looks like boring plumbing — a JSON-RPC socket, a tool list, resources. But that boring plumbing is exactly what turns an LLM from a chat box into a collaborator.
Why MCP is awesome: plumbing that connects the stack
Underneath the slick chat interface lives JSON-RPC, a small server process and a list of tools. That boring machinery is the actual magic.

value.markup:
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard that lets an AI model talk to tools the same way your browser talks to printers: through a protocol almost nobody needs to think about.

A server, a client, three verbs

Clients connect to servers. Servers expose three things:

  • Tools — functions the model can call, declared once, executed anywhere.
  • Resources — data the model can read before it starts answering.
  • Prompts — reusable instruction templates.

That is the whole spec. What makes it valuable is not the list — it is what the list implies: a model can now reach into your CMS, your database and your command line without anyone writing bespoke glue per app.

values.value: Stop thinking of MCP as an API pier. It is a graph: the model, your database, your media library and your CI are all nodes on one protocol.
MCP as a network: every tool a node
Protocols win not because they are elegant but because they connect systems that never expected to meet.
One wire for the whole stack

value.markup:
The easiest way to misread MCP is as yet another API pier: a point where your app meets someone else's. That framing hides the real geometry.

Nodes, not spokes

With MCP, your content management system, your media library, your build pipeline and your vector store all expose the same wire. The model is not a hub the world plugs into — it is one more node on a graph where anything can talk to anything.

  1. A server that can read turns files into resources.
  2. A server that can write turns actions into tools.
  3. A server that can do both becomes infrastructure.

Look at the image block above this post: the picture did not come from an upload form. It came from a folder on disk, read by a media server, picked by a document model, and placed into a block grid member — all over the same protocol that wrote this paragraph.
